The county older school buildings are being surveyed before decisions are taken on their future. Most date from the 1890s and were extended twice in the twentieth century. The survey began in the spring and covers twenty-three sites. The survey is funded by the county heritage office.

Classroom fittings are often the best surviving evidence of daily use. Blackboards, clock cases, and desk rows are recorded room by room, with photographs and measurements. Where a room has been altered, the team records the change and the date if it is known.

Paperwork sometimes survives alongside the furniture. The final lesson plan remained filed beneath the old timetable for decades. Archivists treat such finds as a record of ordinary practice rather than of anything unusual.

Staff records from closed schools are held at the county office. Employment files, registers, and staff-room notices are catalogued together, though gaps are common and are not always explained. Gaps in the staff files are noted but are not treated as evidence of anything by themselves.

The survey team has interviewed former caretakers where possible. Their accounts of routine, and of any unusual event, are recorded separately from the physical survey. The team has also recorded the sound of each building, though this is not part of the formal report.

A final report will recommend which buildings merit listing. Listing would not by itself require the buildings to be opened to the public. No decision has been made about the sites still in use, and the survey will continue into next year.

story.title: The Blackboard in Classroom Seven
story.hook: I was the only person inside the old school that night. From classroom seven came the soft scrape of chalk. The room had been locked for years.
paragraphs: I had worked as the school's caretaker for almost six years. The building closed after the evening shift disappeared. Most rooms stayed locked. I checked the halls after sunset, emptied the bins, and shut off the lights. Classroom seven was always last.

The door had swollen in its frame. I needed both hands to open it. Dust covered the floor in an even grey layer. Nothing had crossed it since the previous winter. At least, nothing that left footprints.

The first time I heard chalk, I blamed the heating pipes. They clicked inside the walls as the temperature fell. Still, the sound came in a steady rhythm. Scratch. Pause. Scratch. It stopped whenever I reached the corridor outside.

The corridor light above the room had begun to flicker. It stayed dark for three seconds, then returned with a weak yellow glow. Each time it came back, the classroom door seemed closer. I measured the distance once. I stopped doing that after.

On the fourth evening, I entered with a lantern. The room smelled of dust and damp plaster. Desks stood in their old rows. A wooden ruler lay beside the teacher's desk, covered in a film of grey powder.
The blackboard was not clean. A surname filled the center of it in tall, narrow letters. I knew the handwriting from old staff records. The evening-shift teacher had used that same careful script.

The teacher vanished during the school's final year. Nobody saw him leave. His coat remained in the staff room, and his bicycle stayed chained outside. People stopped using the word missing after a while. They called him gone.
I wiped the surname away with a damp cloth. White dust gathered in the grooves of the board. When I finished, the cloth was dry. The chalk ledge beneath it was wet enough to leave a shining mark.

I checked the windows. They were painted shut from the inside. The ceiling hatch was sealed with rusted screws. There was no second door. I locked the classroom, then stood in the corridor until the light steadied.

The next morning, I searched the staff records. His final lesson plan was still filed beneath the old timetable. The last line had been crossed out. Beside it, in the margin, he had written, Leave the board until the bell. "The final lesson plan remained filed beneath the old timetable for decades."
There was no bell in the building anymore. The main clock had stopped during the closure. Yet classroom seven had its own small clock above the board. Its hands pointed to the same hour every night.
I went back after dusk and watched from the doorway. The clock remained still. The corridor light blinked once. Then the chalk began moving across the board, though no hand held it.

It wrote the teacher's surname again. The letters appeared slowly, one stroke at a time. I could hear the chalk touch the board. I could also hear breathing near the windows. The windows stayed closed.
At the bottom of the board, a second line appeared. It was not a name. It was the hour written in words. That was the hour when the teacher had vanished. I had seen it in the old report.
The chalk stopped beneath the second line. For several seconds, nothing moved. Then a new word appeared below it. Mine. Not my surname. The name my mother had used before I entered school.
I had never written that name in the caretaker's office. It was not on my records. Only the teacher had known it. He used it once when I started the job, then never spoke to me again.

The classroom clock began to tick. The hands moved backward toward the hour of the disappearance. Behind me, the locked door opened by itself. On the board, the teacher's surname shifted lower, making space above it.
A final line formed at the top. It said, You were absent yesterday. From inside the empty room came the scrape of a chair being pulled across the floor.
I left the lantern on the floor and walked out. I did not run. The corridor light followed me in its broken rhythm. Behind each dark doorway, something made the small sound of chalk being set down.
At the gate, I found white dust on my coat. It covered the sleeves and shoulders. The wind had been blowing toward the school all night. The dust had settled on me from behind.

I returned after sunrise with new locks. Classroom seven was shut. The key turned once, then stopped. From inside came three quiet taps against the door. They followed the rhythm of a lesson beginning.

Since then, the school has stayed empty. I still pass it sometimes before dawn. The windows are black, except for classroom seven. Behind that glass, a pale line appears, then fades before I can read it.
story.ending: I never wiped that board again. The next morning, the classroom door stood open. Every other door in the corridor was locked. Inside, the blackboard was clean except for one wet line beneath the teacher's name. It read, Stay until the lesson ends. I left the school before sunrise. The corridor light flickered behind me, one room at a time. Have you ever heard something like this?

According to the tenancy file, the building on Corvid Row was completed in 1911 and rose six floors above a single stairwell. The roof terrace had been empty for years by 1974, and the access door stayed locked because the latch was broken. A caretaker lived on the ground floor until 1974, when the post passed to the letting office.

Tenants' accounts, collected by the heritage society in 1998, describe the caretaker's chair as wooden, with one short leg that caught on the floor each time it moved. The same accounts say the caretaker used to drag the chair indoors during storms and tie it to the railing on the terrace. No photograph of the chair survives, and the office has no record of it after 1979.

In March 1979 a tenant on the fifth floor reported scraping sounds after midnight. The office replied that the terrace was unused and the door locked. It noted the complaint in one line and took no further action. A second letter, filed four years later, was answered in the same terms.

Later occupants described paint falling from the ceiling above the bed in wet weather. The society inspected the flat in 1998 and found the plaster whole. Pale flakes were recovered from the floor beside the bed and kept with the tenancy papers. The paint had been rubbed away in three places beside the roof door, low and horizontal, and the marks were recorded in the same file.

The chain was still around the handle when the door was inspected in 2006, though the latch had never been repaired. The terrace was resurfaced that summer and the door replaced with a steel panel. Nothing in the file explains the marks, and no tenant has ever been named in connection with them.

story.title: The Chair Above My Ceiling
story.hook: I was the last tenant at the end of the corridor. Every night, a chair dragged above my ceiling. There was only a roof terrace up there.
paragraphs: I rented the flat during a wet summer. The building had six floors and one narrow stairwell. My room sat beneath the roof access. Above me was a locked terrace, used for nothing. The paint inside the building had gone soft from the humidity. It smelled old even after the windows were open.

The first sound came on my third night. It began after midnight. Something scraped across the ceiling above my bed. The noise moved slowly, like wooden legs crossing concrete. It stopped near the far wall. I waited for another sound. Nothing came. Then the scrape began again.

I asked the tenant across from me about it. He listened without looking up from his keys. He said the roof terrace had been empty for years. The access door stayed locked because the latch was broken. He had never heard anything above his flat. Then he shut his door.

The chair dragged at the same hour for four nights. I began leaving the lamp on. The sound always started above the bed. It crossed the ceiling in three long movements. After that, I heard a small pause. The final scrape stopped directly above my pillow.

The smell changed on the fifth night. Old paint filled the room, thick and damp. I found pale flakes on the floor beside my bed. They were not from my ceiling. The plaster above me looked whole. I swept the flakes into a cup and left it by the window.

The next evening, I checked the stairwell. The roof door stood above the sixth floor. Its paint was blistered and yellow. A chain passed through the handle. I touched it once. The metal felt warm, though the stairwell was cooler than my room.

The chair became easier to picture after that. It sounded wooden. One leg caught on the floor each time it moved. I imagined it crossing the terrace in darkness. The thought stayed with me while I worked. At night, I kept my shoes beside the bed.

On the seventh night, the scrape started earlier. It came before the building grew quiet. I went upstairs and stood beside the roof door. The chain trembled on the handle. No wind reached that stairwell. From behind the door came one slow drag.

I noticed marks on the wall beside the door. They were low and horizontal. The paint had been rubbed away in three places. The marks pointed upward, toward the terrace. I placed my hand over one of them. It was damp, and it smelled like the flakes from my room.

The tenant across the hall found me there. He looked at the door and went pale. He told me the chair had belonged to a former caretaker. Years earlier, it had been kept on the roof. He said it was usually tied to the railing before anyone went up.

He also told me something I had not asked. The caretaker used to drag the chair indoors during storms. The chair had one short leg. You could hear it catch on the floor. He had heard that sound from below, long after the caretaker left the building.

That night, the scraping stopped above my pillow. I heard a second sound instead. It came from the corridor outside my door. A wooden leg touched the floor. Then another. The movement ended at my threshold. The handle did not turn.

I went to the roof before dawn. The chain was still around the handle, but it hung loose. The door stood open by several inches. It had opened inward, against the direction of the wind. Old paint smell drifted through the gap.

The terrace was empty at first glance. Then I saw the chair beside the far parapet. It faced the open doorway. One leg rested on a patch of fresh paint. The chair was wet, though the terrace was dry. Behind me, the door moved wider.

A scrape sounded from the middle of the terrace. The chair shifted one short distance toward me. Its damaged leg caught on the concrete. Nothing touched its back. I stepped through the doorway, and the chair stopped.
The door swung shut behind me. The latch clicked from the stairwell side. Across the terrace, the chair faced the place where I stood. Below my feet, another scrape began. It was coming from my room.

I did not cross the terrace. I waited until daylight reached the parapet. The chair remained where it was. When I opened the door again, the chain was hanging in place. The chair was no longer beside the parapet.

It stood outside my flat. The seat faced my door. Pale paint flakes covered the floor around it. I checked every room before touching the handle. Nothing had been disturbed. The chair left no marks on the corridor tiles.

After that morning, the sound changed. It no longer came from above. At midnight, I heard the chair move along the corridor. It stopped outside my door each night. I never opened it. In the morning, it always stood a little closer to the stairs.
story.ending: I moved out before the next rent was due. The corridor stayed quiet while I carried my boxes downstairs. On my last night, I looked back from the entrance. The chair stood at the far end, beneath the peeling light. It faced the stairwell. I still do not know who dragged it there. Have you ever heard something like this?

According to the reports, two cars left a coastal road between Kettle Ness and Barrow Ford in separate years. The weather was clear and dry on both nights, and visibility was recorded as good. Ten years separated the two events. The road section was the same in both cases, though the surface was renewed once in between.

The reports describe one driver in each car, alone on both occasions. The two men lived in different provinces. Neither knew the other, and neither could be interviewed afterwards. A third crash on the same stretch, in rain, involved a passenger and has been kept out of this comparison.

The investigation file records no brake marks near the crash site in either case. At the earlier scene the verge showed no scuffing either; at the later one a broken marker post was found forty metres beyond the barrier. The file notes the difference and does not resolve it.

The first important clue came from the phone records. They place each driver on an incoming call shortly before the crash. According to the later account, both calls came from the same number, and the record does not preserve what was said during either call.

The comparison was reopened in 2022, after an investigator working through digitised files noticed the number. The connection was not found at either original scene, and neither file explains why the calls mattered. The records establish the calls, though they identify no caller.

A review of the two files has been circulated among the traffic units. It recommends that the older report be read alongside the later one, and that the number be traced before any conclusion is drawn. No date has been set for that work.

story.title: The Number Before the Crashes
story.hook: I read two crash reports from the same coastal road. They were written ten years apart, on clear nights, yet both mention an incoming call just before the cars left the road. The reports never identify who made it.
paragraphs: According to the reports, both crashes happened at night. The weather was clear and dry. Visibility was recorded as good. The road section was the same in both cases. Ten years separated the two events.
The reports describe one driver in each car. Neither driver had a passenger. The drivers did not know each other. They lived in different provinces. Neither could be interviewed afterward.

The first report describes an ordinary night on the coast. There was no recorded storm. The road was dry. The surrounding stretch offered few signs of activity. Distant headlights were the only movement noted in the scene.
One detail stood out in the first report. Investigators found no brake marks near the crash site. The road surface showed no sign that the driver had tried to slow before leaving it.
A decade passed before the second crash. Between the two events, the coastal stretch was resurfaced once. The later investigation file records no discussion of that change.
The second report again describes clear weather and good visibility. It also records no brake marks. The same absence appeared at the second site, despite the years between the crashes.

The circumstances also repeated in quieter ways. The second driver was alone. That driver had no known connection to the first. The reports place the two people in separate provinces and separate lives.
The first important clue came from the phone records. They place the first driver on an incoming call shortly before the crash. The record does not preserve what was said during that call.
The second phone record contains the same kind of entry. An incoming call arrived shortly before the second crash. According to the record, it came from the same phone number.
The shared number was not a detail from memory. It appeared in both sets of phone records. Each call came before its corresponding crash. The timing was close enough to bring the files together.

Another detail complicated the comparison. The road had been resurfaced between the crashes. The second file does not mention that work. That omission made the two locations harder to compare by surface evidence alone.
According to the later account, a new investigator noticed the number while digitising old files. The investigator reopened the comparison. The connection was not found at either original scene.
The early investigations had treated the crashes as separate events. The resurfacing was absent from the second file. The shared number appeared only after the older records were compared again.
That later comparison changed the shape of the case. Two unrelated drivers had taken calls from the same number. Both crashed on the same road section. Neither report explains why the calls mattered.
The records establish the calls, but not the caller. They do not show what either driver heard. They do not establish why both cars left the road without brake marks.
The new investigator could reopen the comparison. That did not reopen either driver's account. Both remained unreachable, and the two original reports still contained their separate conclusions.
The drivers left no shared history behind. The reports say they did not know each other. Their lives began in different provinces, then crossed only in records made after the crashes.

The road itself had changed between the two nights. Its surface was replaced once. The absence of brake marks remained in both accounts, but the later file did not preserve every detail needed to place that absence in context.
story.ending: The comparison could connect the two crashes without explaining them. It could identify a pattern without identifying the caller. The road kept its silence, and the number remained only a line in two separate records. What do you think happened before those calls?

According to the file, the case returned twenty years later, after a bundle of statements was transferred from the old courthouse. The bundle had been kept in a damp room, and the first three pages had been replaced during an earlier rebinding.

The original report began on a Thursday afternoon. The missing woman had last been seen the previous evening, and the recorded place was the river market. The file gives no account of her return home. She had lived in the town for three years; no known quarrels were recorded, and no known debts either.

The last witness statement in the bundle is unsigned. It is typed on different paper from the rest of the folder, and the typeface is also different. According to the file, the change was visible when the bundle arrived, and an archivist noted it in the margin.

An early assumption held that the folder had simply preserved an old statement. The bundle showed something else: a page that had been typed later and filed where the original statement belonged. The replacement describes a woman walking away from the river market, gives no hour for the departure, and names no road.

The case was filed by a clerk who retired in 2001. According to the records, he was interviewed twice after the bundle arrived and said he had no memory of the substitution. The interview notes are held with the file.

The unsigned letter that prompted the reopening carried a stamp but no postmark. The newspaper kept no record of who delivered it, and no sender was recorded by the paper. Beyond establishing that a statement was swapped, the file says nothing about who replaced it.

A second review was listed for 2024, and the question attached to that page has not been answered.

story.title: The Page That Replaced the Witness
story.hook: At a dry desk, I read about one page that does not belong. The reopened file carries a replacement statement, typed on different paper.
paragraphs: According to the file, the case returned twenty years later. An unsigned letter had reached the local newspaper. That letter brought the disappearance back into view.
The original report began on a Tuesday morning. The missing man had last been seen two days earlier. The recorded place was the river market.
The file says he had lived in the town for three years. It records no known quarrels. It records no known debts.
The report arrived after the market had closed around him. The file gives no account of his return home. It only fixes the report to that Tuesday morning.
According to the last witness statement, he left the market alone. The statement gives no hour for that departure. The missing hour sits close to the center of the case.
The page describes a man walking away from the river market. It does not describe anyone beside him. It does not place him on a particular road.
The original case was filed by a clerk who later retired. According to the records, that clerk was never interviewed after the letter arrived.
The newspaper kept no record of who delivered the letter. The envelope had no stamp. It had no postmark either.
The file connects the reopening to that unsigned letter. The delivery left no ordinary trail. No sender was recorded by the paper.
A second version of the last witness statement appears in the reopened file. The document is unsigned. Its place in the folder is different from the first account.
The replacement page is on different paper. Its typeface is also different. According to the file, that change was visible when the case was reopened.
The early assumption was that the folder had simply preserved an old statement. The reopened file shows something narrower and stranger. The page was a replacement.
The second statement is not described as a duplicate copy. It appears as another version of the last witness account. The paper and typeface separate it from the page expected there.
The witness account still says the man left alone. It still gives no hour. The clerk who filed the first case was never asked about the change.
The file establishes that a statement was swapped. It does not establish who replaced it, or when.
The missing hour remains unresolved. So does the clerk's unanswered connection to the altered page.
The letter reopened the case, but it did not identify its sender. The newspaper could only preserve the envelope and its silence.
The clerk had already retired when the letter arrived. The file records no later interview. That absence leaves the old filing process unexamined.
The records offer no known quarrel or debt involving the missing man. They offer a departure, a missing hour, and two versions of one statement. The river keeps the rest outside the file.
story.ending: The file leaves the river market behind, but not the question attached to that page. What do you think happened before the statement was replaced?

There are nine shrines along the mountain road between Kestrel Pass and Low Water. Most are no more than a roof over a stone shelf, with a narrow lamp inside. Drivers who used the road before it was widened told the same story in different words: stop, leave water, say nothing.

The ethnographers who recorded the shrines in 2011 noted one at the fourth bend, where the flame had gone out but the wick still smelled of smoke. The lamp was lit again in 2014 and has stayed lit since. A brass cup rested behind the shelf, and a dark line circled its rim. The cup was not photographed before it disappeared.

The most complete account came from a bus driver who worked the route for nineteen years. He described a dry voice near the trees asking for water on the next trip, and said he answered without thinking. He also said the crickets stopped whenever he opened the cab door, and the silence lasted until the engine started.

Drivers speak of small footprints in the dust beside the shelf. The prints are described as small and bare, beginning at the water and ending at the edge of the road. No cast has ever been taken. One driver followed them for a few steps and found they faded where the ground turned hard.

On the next trip the bottle he had left was full again, though the cap was sealed and his own bottle was empty in the cab. He spoke of paying a debt he had not contracted, and of a promise made by another driver years earlier, before the road was widened.

The shrine at the fourth bend is kept by the parish. Bottles are still left there, and the dust around the shelf is swept once a year. The parish has no record of the cup, and no one has asked to see the prints.

story.title: The Bottle Left at the Shrine
story.hook: The bottle was full when I returned to the shrine. I had left it empty three trips before. Small footprints crossed the dust beside it.
paragraphs: I drove long routes between industrial towns and mountain passes. That road had few lights after sunset. I stopped beside the shrine because my eyes needed rest.
It was hardly more than a roof over a stone shelf. A narrow lamp sat inside. The flame had gone out, but the wick still smelled of smoke.
I had one bottle left in the cab. I placed it beneath the shelf. The night was cool enough to keep the water clear.
Before I left, I heard a dry voice near the trees. It asked for water on the next trip. I looked around, but saw only branches moving above the road.
I answered without thinking. I said I would bring another bottle. Then I climbed back into the cab and drove until dawn.
The next morning, I remembered the bottle. I pictured it sitting under the roof. I also remembered the promise, though I could not remember who had asked.
On my return, I brought two bottles. One was for me. One was for the voice. I placed the second beneath the shelf and accepted the same duty again.
The road kept drawing me past that place. Every trip ended near the same hour. I began carrying an extra bottle before I reached the hills.
I never saw anyone waiting there. Still, the crickets stopped whenever I opened the cab door. Their silence lasted until the engine started.
The third time, I noticed prints beside the shelf. They were small and bare. They began at the water and ended at the edge of the road.
I followed them for a few steps. They faded where the ground turned hard. No grass was bent. No stone had shifted.
An old brass cup rested behind the bottle. I had not seen it before. A dark line circled its rim, as though someone had filled it many times.
On the next trip, I found my bottle full again. The cap was still sealed. My own bottle was empty in the cab.
The prints surrounded the shelf. They crossed over mine and returned toward the trees. The voice came from there again, softer than before.
It asked why I had stopped bringing the water I owed. I said I had brought it every time. The crickets began calling from much closer.
In the cab mirror, the shrine stood behind me. A second shape occupied the doorway. I saw only a small hand resting against the frame.
The lamp inside lit by itself. The bottle on the shelf tipped toward the doorway. The footprints led away from it, toward the road I had just traveled.
The voice named the debt then. Years earlier, another driver had promised water before leaving that road. He never returned. I was paying what he had left behind.
I stayed until morning. I did not sleep. At first light, I placed every bottle from the cab beneath the shelf.
The small prints appeared once more. They crossed the clearing and stopped at the road. After that, they never came back.
The brass cup disappeared with them. Only a pale ring remained on the stone. I wiped it away before starting the engine.
For several months, I avoided that route. The longer roads cost more fuel. They also left me with the sound of crickets in every rest stop.
Then one evening, I found a full bottle on the passenger seat. I had locked the cab. The seal was unbroken, and dust covered the cap.
story.ending: I still stop there when the road takes me past. I bring water before I bring anything else. The dust stays smooth now. The bottle stays empty. I never learned whose thirst I answered, only that the promise is settled. What would you have done?

Vào sáng ngày mười bốn, người bán hàng ở chợ Bến Cá phát hiện quầy vàng của bà Trần Thị Mến đã bị cạy mở từ phía sau. Khóa vẫn còn nguyên trên cửa, nhưng bản lề đã bị tháo ra và đặt lại rất gọn gàng. Bà Mến nói rằng bà chỉ rời quầy chưa đầy một giờ để đi lấy hàng.

Đội điều tra do ông Hồ Văn Lực phụ trách bắt đầu từ những chiếc đinh vít. Các đinh vít trên bản lề đều là loại mới, không khớp với phần còn lại của khung cửa. Ông Lực cho rằng người lấy đã thay bản lề trước, rồi quay lại tháo chúng trong đêm.

Camera ở đầu hẻm chỉ ghi được một bóng người mặc áo mưa đi ngược chiều gió. Hình ảnh mờ đến mức không thể nhận dạng, nhưng thời gian trên máy lại khớp với lúc bà Mến rời chợ. Ông Lực ghi chú rằng người đó không mang theo túi, dù số vàng mất đi nặng gần hai ký.

Hồ sơ vụ án không ghi tên người tố giác. Ông Lực cho rằng người này có thể là một tiểu thương trong chợ, vì chỉ người quen mới biết giờ bà Mến rời quầy. Ông đã hỏi mười hai người và không ai nhận mình là người báo.

Ba tuần sau, một tiệm cầm đồ ở thị trấn bên kia sông báo có người đến bán một sợi dây chuyền khắc tên bà Mến. Người bán khai rằng mình nhặt được dây chuyền trong bãi đất trống sau chợ. Ông Lực cho người kiểm tra bãi đất và tìm thấy một chiếc hộp thiếc chôn nông, bên trong là bốn chiếc đinh vít mới.

Vụ án khép lại mà không ai bị kết tội. Người bán dây chuyền không bị truy tố vì không đủ chứng cứ, còn chiếc hộp thiếc thì được giữ trong kho tang vật. Một ghi chú cuối hồ sơ của ông Lực viết rằng cánh cửa đó đã được tháo ra hai lần, và lần thứ hai không để lại dấu vết nào.

story.title: The Stall Behind the Market
story.hook: On the morning of the fourteenth, a vendor at Ben Ca market found that the gold stall of Mrs Tran Thi Men had been prised open from behind. The lock was still on the door, but the hinges had been removed and put back very neatly. Mrs Men said she had left the stall for less than an hour to collect goods.
paragraphs: The investigation, led by Mr Ho Van Luc, began with the screws. Every screw in the hinges was new and did not match the rest of the door frame. Mr Luc believed the thief had replaced the hinges first and then come back in the night to take them out.

The camera at the top of the alley recorded only a figure in a raincoat walking against the wind. The image was too blurred to identify anyone, but the timestamp matched the hour Mrs Men left the market. Mr Luc noted that the figure carried no bag, although nearly two kilos of gold had gone.

The case file does not name the person who reported it. Mr Luc believed it could be a trader in the market, because only someone familiar would know the hour Mrs Men left her stall. He questioned twelve people, and none admitted to making the report.

Three weeks later, a pawnshop in the town across the river reported that someone had come to sell a necklace engraved with Mrs Men's name. The seller said he had found the necklace on the waste ground behind the market. Mr Luc sent men to search the ground and they found a tin buried shallow, with four new screws inside.
story.ending: The case closed without anyone being convicted. The seller of the necklace was not prosecuted for lack of evidence, and the tin was kept in the property store. A final note in Mr Luc's file says that the door had been taken apart twice, and that the second time left no trace at all.

source.text:
Phòng trọ cuối dãy của bà Tư nằm sát bức tường gạch của xóm Rạch Vàng. Căn phòng trống gần hai năm vì không ai chịu thuê lâu. Sinh viên thuê trước đã dọn đi trong một đêm, để lại đèn vẫn sáng và cửa không khóa.

Người thuê mới tên Hạnh, làm ở tiệm may đầu chợ. Đêm thứ ba, Hạnh nghe thấy ba tiếng gõ đều nhau trên vách tường cạnh giường. Cô gõ lại hai tiếng để thử, và nhận được đúng hai tiếng đáp lại. Bà Tư nói bức tường đó là tường ngoài, phía sau chỉ có rãnh nước.

Hạnh nhờ bà Tư ngủ nhờ một đêm trong phòng. Bà Tư đồng ý, nhưng đến nửa đêm bà đã ra ngoài ngồi ở bậc cửa. Sáng hôm sau, bà nói rằng bà không nghe thấy gì, và từ đó bà không nhắc đến chuyện tiếng gõ nữa.

Hạnh kê lại giường sang phía cửa. Tiếng gõ đi theo cô, vẫn đúng ba tiếng, vẫn đúng khoảng cách. Cô nhờ người bạn đứng bên kia rãnh nước để nghe, nhưng bạn cô chỉ thấy tường gạch và một hàng chậu vỡ. Tối đó, tiếng gõ ngừng hẳn.

Bà Tư kể rằng trước đây có một người đàn ông sống ở phòng đó, chuyên sửa khóa cho cả xóm. Ông ta mất trong một trận lụt, khi đang cố mở cửa cho người bên trong. Từ đó, khách thuê thường nghe tiếng gõ, nhưng chỉ những người ngủ một mình mới nghe rõ.

Hạnh dọn đi vào cuối tháng, để lại chiếc chìa khóa trên bàn và một tờ giấy ghi hai chữ trả lại. Bà Tư treo tờ giấy lên vách, chỗ tiếng gõ vẫn còn vang mỗi khi trời mưa. Căn phòng đến nay vẫn chưa có người thuê mới.

story.title: The Knocking on the Back Wall
story.hook: The last room in Mrs Tu's row of rented rooms stood against the brick wall of Rach Vang hamlet. The room had been empty for nearly two years because nobody would stay long. The student who rented it before had moved out in a single night, leaving the light on and the door unlocked.
paragraphs: The new tenant was Hanh, who worked at the tailor's shop at the head of the market. On the third night, Hanh heard three evenly spaced knocks on the wall beside the bed. She knocked twice in reply to test it, and received exactly two knocks back. Mrs Tu said that wall was an outer wall, and that behind it there was only a drainage channel.

Hanh asked Mrs Tu to sleep one night in the room. Mrs Tu agreed, but by midnight she had gone outside to sit on the step. The next morning she said she had heard nothing, and after that she never mentioned the knocking again.

Hanh moved the bed towards the door. The knocking followed her, still three knocks, still the same interval. She asked a friend to stand on the other side of the channel and listen, but her friend saw only brick and a row of broken pots. That evening, the knocking stopped altogether.

Mrs Tu said that a man had once lived in that room, a locksmith who repaired locks for the whole hamlet. He had died in a flood while trying to open a door for the people inside. Since then, tenants often heard knocking, but only those who slept alone heard it clearly.
story.ending: Hanh moved out at the end of the month, leaving the key on the table and a note with two words: give it back. Mrs Tu hung the note on the wall, where the knocking still sounds whenever it rains. The room has still not found a new tenant.

source.text:
Làng Đồng Vẹt không có đình lớn, chỉ có một miếu nhỏ dựng bên bờ kênh. Mỗi năm vào tháng tư, dân làng làm lễ cầu mưa và không ai được mang giày vào miếu. Người lớn nói rằng đất trong miếu là đất của thần, không phải đất của người.

Lễ do bà Đồng Thị Lụa đứng ra sắp xếp suốt bốn mươi năm. Bà chuẩn bị xôi, hoa và một chén nước mưa hứng từ mái miếu. Trước khi cúng, bà đi một vòng quanh miếu và gọi tên từng người đã mất trong năm cũ. Bà giữ danh sách những người đã mất trong một cuốn sổ nhỏ, và năm nào cũng đọc lại từ đầu.

Trong làng có tục để lại một chiếc nón lá ở cửa miếu cho người đi xa. Ai về làng thì lấy nón của mình, ai không về thì chiếc nón ở lại qua mùa. Đến cuối năm, những chiếc nón không có người nhận được đốt cùng giấy vàng.

Người làng còn giữ một chiếc chiếu cũ để trải trước cửa miếu vào ngày lễ. Chiếc chiếu chỉ được dùng một lần mỗi năm, và không ai được giặt nó. Năm nào mưa đến sớm, người ta vẫn trải chiếu rồi mới dọn vào.

Năm lụt lớn, nước dâng đến bậc miếu nhưng không vào bên trong. Dân làng kể rằng bà Lụa đứng suốt đêm trên bậc, tay cầm chén nước mưa, và nước đã dừng lại trước chân bà. Chuyện đó không ai ghi lại, chỉ truyền miệng qua mấy đời.

Bà Lụa mất vào mùa khô năm sau. Lễ vẫn được tổ chức, nhưng người làng chia nhau việc chuẩn bị thay vì để một người làm. Chiếc nón của bà vẫn treo ở cửa miếu, và không ai dám lấy xuống.

story.title: The Rain Ceremony at Dong Vet
story.hook: Dong Vet village has no large communal house, only a small shrine built beside the canal. Every year in the fourth month, the villagers hold a ceremony to ask for rain, and nobody may wear shoes inside the shrine. The adults say that the ground inside the shrine belongs to the spirit, not to people.
paragraphs: Mrs Dong Thi Lua organised the ceremony for forty years. She prepared sticky rice, flowers and a bowl of rainwater caught from the shrine roof. Before the offering, she walked once around the shrine and spoke the names of everyone who had died in the past year. She kept the list of the dead in a small notebook, and read it from the beginning every year.

The village has a custom of leaving a conical hat at the shrine door for anyone who travels far. Whoever returns takes their own hat; whoever does not return leaves the hat through the season. At the end of the year, the hats with no one to claim them are burned with paper gold.

The village also keeps an old mat to spread in front of the shrine on the day of the ceremony. The mat is used only once a year, and nobody may wash it. In years when the rain comes early, the mat is still spread before it is taken in.

In the year of the great flood, the water rose to the shrine step but did not go inside. The villagers say that Mrs Lua stood on the step all night with the bowl of rainwater in her hands, and the water stopped before her feet. Nobody wrote that story down; it was only passed by word of mouth through several generations.
story.ending: Mrs Lua died in the dry season the following year. The ceremony is still held, but the villagers share the preparations instead of leaving them to one person. Her hat still hangs at the shrine door, and nobody dares to take it down.

source.text:
Bến Cồn Sậy chỉ có một cây cầu gỗ và ba chiếc thuyền câu. Người dân ở đây nói rằng ai đi câu sau nửa đêm thì phải mang theo một nắm muối. Muối để rắc xuống nước trước khi thả câu, không phải để mồi cá.

Ông Nguyễn Văn Hòa đi câu đêm suốt hai mươi năm và chưa từng gặp chuyện gì. Một đêm tháng chín, ông nghe tiếng mái chèo khua nước phía sau thuyền, dù bến đã đóng cửa từ chiều. Ông quay lại thì chỉ thấy mặt nước phẳng và chiếc lồng cá của mình đang trôi ngược dòng.

Ông Hòa kể rằng đêm đó không có gió, và mặt sông phẳng như tấm ván. Ông đã câu ở bến này từ khi còn trẻ, nên ông biết tiếng nước nào là tiếng cá. Tiếng mái chèo đó không giống bất cứ âm thanh nào ông từng nghe.

Ông Hòa chèo vào bờ và kể lại cho người giữ bến. Người này mở sổ ghi thuyền ra, chỉ vào một dòng từ năm trước: một chiếc thuyền câu mất tích cùng người chèo, không tìm thấy xác. Ông Hòa nhận ra chiếc lồng trôi ngược dòng chính là lồng của chiếc thuyền đó. Ông hỏi tên người chèo thuyền, nhưng người giữ bến không trả lời.

Từ đêm ấy, ông Hòa chỉ đi câu khi trời còn sáng. Ông vẫn rắc muối xuống nước, nhưng rắc ở mũi thuyền thay vì giữa dòng. Những người câu khác trong bến làm theo ông mà không ai giải thích được vì sao.

Chiếc lồng cá được treo ở vách nhà người giữ bến, không ai dám mang về dùng. Mùa mưa năm sau, nước dâng làm chiếc lồng rơi xuống sông. Người ta tìm lại được nó ở đúng chỗ ông Hòa nghe thấy tiếng mái chèo.

story.title: The Man Who Fished at Night
story.hook: Con Say landing has only one wooden bridge and three fishing boats. The people here say that anyone who fishes after midnight must carry a handful of salt. The salt is scattered on the water before the lines go in, and it is not for the fish.
paragraphs: Mr Nguyen Van Hoa had fished at night for twenty years and had never met anything strange. One night in September, he heard the sound of an oar stirring water behind his boat, although the landing had been closed since the afternoon. When he turned, he saw only flat water, and his own fish trap drifting upstream.

Mr Hoa said there was no wind that night, and the river lay as flat as a board. He had fished at this landing since he was young, so he knew which sounds belonged to fish. That oar did not resemble any sound he had heard before.

Mr Hoa rowed to the bank and told the man who kept the landing. The man opened the boat register and pointed to a line from the year before: a fishing boat had disappeared with its rower, and no body was found. Mr Hoa realised that the trap drifting upstream was the trap from that boat. He asked the name of the rower, but the landing keeper did not answer.

After that night, Mr Hoa fished only while the light lasted. He still scattered salt on the water, but at the bow of the boat instead of midstream. The other fishermen at the landing copied him, and none of them could explain why.
story.ending: The fish trap was hung on the wall of the landing keeper's house, and nobody dared take it home to use. The following rainy season, the water rose and the trap fell into the river. It was found again in exactly the place where Mr Hoa had heard the oar.

source.text:
The fog signal on the south pier was installed to warn boats away from the shoal. It ran on compressed air and a brass timer, and it sounded once every ninety seconds. The last keeper of the signal, a man named Orin Vale, kept a diary of its failures in a drawer beneath the console.

Vale's diary begins in October, with a week of ordinary entries. The air tanks held pressure. The timer advanced. The horn sounded on schedule. On the eighth night he wrote that the signal had sounded twice within a minute, though the timer still showed a single mark. He checked the pressure gauge twice before writing the entry.

By November the pattern had changed again. The horn sounded only when the tide turned, and then it kept sounding until the pressure failed. Vale replaced the timer spring and cleaned the valve seats. He recorded every repair in the same narrow script, and each repair was followed by one night of silence. He kept the replaced parts in a tin box and labelled each one with the date.

The harbour office sent an inspector in December. The inspector found the console in good order and the tanks half full. He interviewed two fishermen who claimed to have heard the horn from the far side of the bay. Neither could say how a disconnected compressor had produced a sound at all. His report was filed with the harbour board and copied to the town council.

The signal was removed in the spring and the pier was closed to visitors. Vale's diary was donated to the town library, where it is kept in a locked cabinet. A note on the first page warns that the diary was not written in order. The final entry is dated a year after the signal came down.

source.text:
The Blunt Street inquiry opened after a pawnbroker reported a set of stolen spoons. The spoons were ordinary hotel silver, but their owner had reported them missing four years earlier. The report reached a detective named Mara Quill, who had been reviewing unsolved warehouse thefts along the river.

Quill began with the pawn tickets. Every ticket from the same shop carried a small mark in the corner, a practice the owner denied teaching anyone. She traced the marks to a former clerk who had left the shop in debt. His address was a room above a brass foundry on Blunt Street. The landlord remembered him paying in coins.

The foundry kept two sets of ledgers. The first recorded scrap metal bought and sold. The second, hidden inside a crate of moulds, listed items by description rather than weight. Quill counted forty-one entries in the second ledger, each matched to a theft reported over six years. None of the entries used a name, and each was written in the same slanting hand.

The clerk was arrested at the foundry gate with a key ring in his coat. He said the keys belonged to a relative. The relative, when questioned, said the opposite. Quill filed both statements and continued with the ledgers, which she considered more reliable than either man. She also asked the foundry to keep its moulds locked. The key ring held eleven keys, none of which fitted a door at the foundry.

The trial lasted nine days and produced no conviction on the theft charges. The clerk was sentenced only for handling stolen goods, and he left the city after his release. Quill's case notes were returned to the archive with a single page missing. The missing page is still listed in the archive's index, and the index is the only copy.

source.text:
At Osen Ford, the dead are remembered with paper lanterns rather than graves. Families write a name on each lantern and set it on the water at dusk. The current carries the lanterns under the old bridge and out of sight before the church bells ring.

The custom is said to have begun after a flood took the ford's mill and four of its millers. The parish could not recover the bodies, so the miller's widow made lanterns for each missing man and floated them downstream. Other families copied her, and the practice spread to the neighbouring villages. It reached the coast within two generations.

Lantern makers use a frame of split bamboo and a paper skin brushed with wax. The wax matters, the makers say, because an unwaxed lantern sinks before it clears the bridge. Names are written in ink mixed with ash from the household hearth, so that each lantern carries something of the house it came from. The ink is made the same day it is used.

Visitors often ask why the lanterns are not collected. The answer given by the parish is that a lantern belongs to the water once it is released. Anyone who fishes one out must return it the following year with a second name written beside the first. Few visitors attempt this twice. The parish keeps a box of blank lanterns for the purpose.

The festival was suspended during the war and revived in 1949 with fewer families taking part. It has continued every year since, always on the first dry evening after the harvest. The parish keeps no record of the names released. The parish clerk writes the date of each festival in a ledger kept beside the font. Those who write them are expected to remember, and most of them do.

source.text:
Corder's Mill ran three shifts until the grain contract moved north in 1962. The night shift was the smallest, usually six workers and one supervisor. They kept a chalk board by the loading door to record which silos had been emptied.

The mill's last supervisor, a woman named Ellen Marsh, wrote a short account of her final year. She described a sound like a sack dragged across the floor above the loading bay. The upper floor had been cleared for repairs and held nothing but scaffolding. Two workers heard the same sound on the same night. The account runs to four pages and was written in the year after the mill closed. Each silo had a number painted in white above its door.

Marsh sent two workers to check the noise on separate nights. Both returned without finding anything, and both asked to be moved to the day shift. One of them left the mill within a month. The other stayed until the contract ended. Neither would talk about it afterwards. Marsh did not record what she thought of their requests.

The chalk board is mentioned repeatedly in Marsh's account. She wrote that the board was wiped clean each morning and found marked again by the afternoon. The marks were not names or numbers. They were short vertical lines, grouped in fives, as though someone were counting shifts. Marsh counted them too and wrote the totals in the margin.

The mill closed that winter and the machinery was sold for scrap. Marsh's account was typed and filed with the company papers, where it remained unread for thirty years. A photocopy now hangs in the local museum beside a photograph of the night shift. The museum has never been able to identify the missing worker. In the photograph, the chalk board is turned to the wall, and the shift is one worker short.

A photocopy now hangs in the local museum beside a photograph of the night shift. The museum has never been able to identify the missing person.
story.ending: In the photograph, the chalk board is turned to the wall, and the shift is one worker short.

source.text:
The harbour board ordered a full survey of the northern light in the spring of 1968, after three keepers reported that the lantern had burned without fuel. The survey was led by an engineer named Alaric Penn, who had spent eleven years repairing coastal signals along the same stretch of rock. His notebook survives in the county archive, and it remains the only technical account of the tower written while the lamp was still in use.

Penn opened the lantern housing and found the burner dry. The wick had been trimmed, the reservoir cleaned, and the brass fittings polished, none of which explained the glow. He measured the cable run twice and recorded no current at either end. The mechanism, he wrote, was in better condition than the building that housed it. He sealed the room and returned the next morning to find the glass warm.

The survey continued through the winter. Penn tested the tower's earthing, the salt damage on the ironwork, and the alignment of the lantern room windows. He found the windows fixed in place and the frames sound. His drawings show a small hatch behind the lamp, though no later survey mentions it.

Penn's notebook ends without a conclusion. The last pages list materials for a repair that was never carried out, and a note that the board had asked him to stop work. The lighthouse was automated in the following decade and the lantern was removed.

The notebook was deposited with the archive in 1979 by Penn's daughter. A reader's ticket from the same year is still inside the cover, and the pages opposite the entry for the dry burner have been cut out. The archive has never established who removed them.

story.title: The Keeper's Last Entry
story.hook: I kept the lamp in a room above the waves. Each night, I wrote down when it turned itself on. The fuse had been pulled for a week.
paragraphs: I was the keeper of a small lighthouse on the northern coast. The tower stood beyond a stretch of black rock. Salt stayed on the windows, even after the rain stopped. My work was simple. I checked the lantern, trimmed the wick, and recorded every fault in a clothbound log.

The lamp had been unreliable since I arrived. It gave one dull flash after midnight. Then it went dark again. I blamed damp wiring and old fittings. The previous keeper had warned me about the weather. He had not mentioned the lamp.

I began writing down the nights it happened. The first entry took only one line. Lamp lit at half past one. Fuse intact. The next morning, the bulb was cold. There was no smell of smoke. The switch rested exactly where I had left it.

The sound outside changed whenever the lamp came on. Waves struck the rocks below the tower. Then their noise thinned away. It faded until the room seemed sealed from the sea. I could still see the water through the glass. I simply could not hear it.

Penn opened the lantern housing and found the burner dry. The wick had been trimmed, the reservoir cleaned, and the brass fittings polished, none of which explained the glow. He measured the cable run twice and recorded no current at either end. The mechanism, he wrote, was in better condition than the building that housed it. He sealed the room and returned the next morning to find the glass warm.

The lamp came on before dawn. I heard the click above me. The sound passed through the ceiling and into the bed frame. I opened the tin box. The fuse was still inside. Water had gathered beneath it, though the room was dry.

I searched the keeper's cupboard for older records. Behind a row of cracked mugs, I found another log. Its cover had swollen from damp. The pages stopped halfway through winter. Every entry described the same silence after the lamp lit.
The final entry in that older log was written in a narrow hand. It said the lamp was not drawing power. It was answering a signal. Beneath that line, someone had written, Do not let it see the shore.

I thought the line meant the lamp should not face the water. The lantern room had three windows, all fixed in place. I covered the largest one with a canvas sheet. That night, the light appeared behind the cloth.

The glow was weak at first. It pulsed through the canvas like a hand passing behind it. I pulled the sheet down. Beyond the glass, the sea was black and flat. Something pale stood far out on the water, where the waves should have been.

I could not make out a face or a body. I saw only a vertical shape, steady against the dark. The lamp brightened once. The shape moved closer without disturbing the water. Then the sound of the sea began fading again.

I ran downstairs and opened my log. The page had been left blank when I checked it earlier. Now a fresh line crossed the paper. It was not in my handwriting. The ink was wet, and the words were simple. You have kept it waiting.

The lamp went dark. In that instant, the shape stood on the balcony outside the lantern room. The door behind me opened by itself. On the last page, another sentence appeared beneath the first. The keeper must finish the record.

I never touched the balcony door. I went down the stairs with the log under my coat. Every step gave a soft wooden knock. Above me, the lamp came on again. The glow followed me through the tower, shining beneath each closed door.

At the entrance, I found wet marks across the floor. They began at the threshold and ended beside the fuse box. The marks were narrow and uneven. None led back outside. The sea remained silent beyond the walls.
I opened the fuse box. The tin box was inside it. I had left it beside my bed. The fuse rested in the box, covered in salt. A faint warmth came from the metal door.

I took the log and left before sunrise. The path down the rocks was slick with rain. Behind me, the lantern kept turning. Its beam crossed the water and returned. Each time it passed, the waves sounded farther away.

At the foot of the hill, I stopped beside an old marker stone. The lighthouse stood above me, dark except for its lamp. I looked down at the log. The last page was filled now. The writing had changed.

The new lines described the path I had taken. They described the marker stone. They even described the coat around my shoulders. The final line had not been written yet. I closed the book and walked toward the road.
story.ending: I left the log beneath the lamp and walked toward the shore. Behind me, the glass chimney clicked as it cooled. The sea had gone quiet enough to hear the pages turning. I did not look back. I still have the key to that lighthouse, though I have never found the door it opens. Have you ever heard something like this?

source.text:
The city's building office reopened the file on the Marrow Street tenements in 1974, after a tenant complained that furniture was moving above her flat. The complaint had been filed three times before anyone visited. Each visit confirmed the same arrangement of vents, drains and empty concrete. The file carried no photograph until the fourth visit.

The inspector found a single wooden chair on the terrace, facing the stairwell door. Its legs had left four pale tracks in the dust, and the tracks pointed away from the roof hatch. He noted that the chair could not have been carried up the stairwell without striking the walls. The hatch chain was intact and the padlock showed no fresh scratches. He photographed the tracks and wrote that he could offer no explanation for their direction.

The survey continued indoors. The tenants' rooms shared one ceiling, and the joists above them carried sound in unexpected ways. Warm air from the vents made the old plaster tick at night. The report recommended new insulation and a new chain for the roof hatch.

The building office closed the case without a finding. A note in the margin records that the inspector returned twice on his own time. The second visit is not described in the file, but a pencil sketch of the chair was folded behind the final page.

The tenements were demolished in 1981 and the site is now a car park. The file survives in the municipal archive, and the sketch is still folded inside it. Staff who have handled the folder say the pencil lines have darkened over the years, which the archive cannot explain.

story.title: The Chair Above My Ceiling
story.hook: I lived at the end of a narrow corridor. Every night, a chair dragged across the ceiling above me. There was only a locked roof terrace up there.
paragraphs: The building was old enough to hold heat after sunset. Paint lifted in thin curls along the walls. My room sat beneath the roof access. Above it was a flat terrace, empty except for vents and a rusted drain.

The first sound came during my second week. It began with one scrape near the window. Then came three shorter scrapes toward the door. The noise stopped there. I blamed loose furniture in another apartment.
The next night, it came at the same hour. I was lying in bed with the window open. Humid air pressed against the curtains. Underneath it, I could smell old paint, warm plaster, and something dusty.
I asked the tenant across the hall about it. He listened without looking at the ceiling. Then he told me the floor above had no rooms. He said the roof door had been locked since before he moved in.
That evening, I checked the stairwell. The roof door had a chain looped through its handle. Dust covered the threshold. Nothing marked it except a pale line where the door had rubbed the floor.

The scraping returned after midnight. It sounded closer than before. I heard the chair cross the ceiling, pause, and move back again. Each pass ended directly above my bed. The old paint smell filled the room.
I slept in the sitting room for three nights. The sound followed me there. It crossed above the sofa instead. The pattern stayed the same. One long drag, three short ones, then silence.

The landlord sent a maintenance worker to inspect the ceiling. He found no pipes, loose boards, or animals. Before leaving, he glanced toward the stairwell. He asked whether the noise had begun after I moved in.
I asked what he meant. He only said the last tenant had complained about furniture moving overhead. That tenant had left without collecting his deposit. The worker refused to say anything else.
The following night, I placed a glass on the bedroom floor. I wanted to hear whether the scraping came through the room or the ceiling. At midnight, the glass trembled before the first sound began.
The chair dragged from the window side again. This time, I heard a faint knock beneath the scrape. It came three times. The knocks matched the sound I made when testing the roof door.
I went upstairs and stood below the roof access. The chain was still in place. I touched the handle. Above me, something dragged once across the terrace. Then the chain gave a soft metallic rattle.

The inspector found a single wooden chair on the terrace, facing the stairwell door. Its legs had left four pale tracks in the dust, and the tracks pointed away from the roof hatch. He noted that the chair could not have been carried up the stairwell without striking the walls. The hatch chain was intact and the padlock showed no fresh scratches. He photographed the tracks and wrote that he could offer no explanation for their direction.

I asked what was there. He rubbed paint dust from his fingers. Years earlier, someone had carried a chair upstairs during a heat wave. Nobody remembered bringing it back down. After that, tenants heard it moving.

The story sounded ridiculous in daylight. Yet the marks beneath the door looked fresh. Four narrow tracks crossed the dust inside the threshold. They pointed outward, toward the stairwell, not inward toward the terrace.
That night, the scraping began earlier. It crossed above my room, then stopped. I waited with my shoes on. The old paint smell thickened around me. From the ceiling came one careful knock.
I picked up my keys and climbed. The corridor behind me was empty. At the top landing, the chain hung loose. The roof door stood open by the width of a hand.
The door had opened from the inside. I could see the chain lying beyond the threshold. Warm air moved through the gap, carrying the smell of old paint. Something scraped across the terrace.
The terrace held one wooden chair. It faced the open doorway. As I watched, its legs shifted across the concrete and stopped just inside the light.

I did not step onto the terrace. The chair remained still for several seconds. Then it turned toward the stairwell without lifting from the ground. The scraping sound traveled down through the building.
I ran back to my room and locked the door. The sound stopped above me. A moment later, the chair dragged across the corridor outside my apartment. It stopped on the other side of my door.
There was no knock. I watched the handle until morning. At sunrise, I opened the door. Four thin tracks crossed the dust outside, leading toward the stairs.
The roof door was closed again. The chain hung through its handle. On the terrace, the chair was gone. I never learned whether it had returned upstairs, or whether it had only been waiting outside.
story.ending: I moved out before the month was over. The new tenant asked why I left. I told him the ceiling carried sound from the roof. He laughed, then asked if I had heard the chair. I had not told him about the chair. Have you ever heard something like this?

source.text:
In the upland villages, a house key was rarely a private object. Neighbours kept copies in clay jars, and a returning family could ask any door for shelter. The folklore archive recorded eleven such key customs before the practice faded in the 1980s. Most of the accounts came from women who had moved away and returned late in life.

The oldest account came from a woman who had left her village at nineteen. She carried her mother's key for forty years without ever unlocking the house. When she finally returned, the door opened easily, and the rooms smelled of incense that had not been burned there in decades. She told the archivist that the key had grown warm in her pocket during the journey. The archivist noted the detail without comment.

Keys were often buried with the dead or thrown into wells after a sale. Some families kept a waiting key on a nail beside the door, unused, so that the house would not be considered abandoned. The archive has photographs of nine such keys, each with the name of a village painted on a card behind it.

The archive treats these stories as custom rather than history. Its preface warns that a remembered key often stands for a promise that was never kept. The compilers kept no record of their own visits, and the dates on the cards are uneven.

A second volume was planned but never published. Its draft notes are held with the collection and consist mostly of crossings-out. One surviving sentence reads that the keys were collected from houses, not from people, which the present editor interprets as a caution about ownership.

story.title: The Key She Left Behind
story.hook: For ten years, I promised my mother I would take her home. She died before I kept that promise. Since then, I dream of our village house with every light burning, while its key stays in my pocket.
paragraphs: I had carried that key through every rented room. It was small, darkened with age, and warm from my hand. My mother kept it beneath her pillow after we moved away. She said the village house was waiting for us. I told her we would return when work became easier.

Work became a chain of ordinary excuses. One project ended, and another began. Rent rose. Trains ran late. My mother stopped asking for a date. She only folded our old village clothes into a wooden trunk. Each time I saw it, I promised again.

The city apartment was always warm at night. That warmth came from the kitchen, the pipes, and the traffic below. Still, it carried the smell of burnt incense. My mother burned one stick before sleep. She said the scent reminded her of the house.

The first dream came during my third year in the city. I stood outside the village house. Its windows glowed behind the trees. The door was unlocked. Inside, I heard a chair move across the floor. Then my mother called my childhood name.

I woke with the key pressed into my palm. My mother was asleep in the next room. Incense smoke drifted beneath her door. I almost drove back that morning. Instead, my manager called before sunrise. I stayed, and the dream returned the following night.

Years earlier, my mother had placed the key in my hand. Her fingers were thin, but her grip was firm. She made me promise to unlock the house before she died. I laughed then. I told her the house had waited this long.
She did not laugh with me. She asked me to say the promise again. I said I would take her back. I said we would sleep beneath the old ceiling. Then I put the key in my pocket and went to work.

The oldest account came from a woman who had left her village at nineteen. She carried her mother's key for forty years without ever unlocking the house. When she finally returned, the door opened easily, and the rooms smelled of incense that had not been burned there in decades. She told the archivist that the key had grown warm in her pocket during the journey. The archivist noted the detail without comment.

After ten years, my mother died in the city. We held the quiet funeral near the apartment. That night, the village house appeared again. Every window was lit. The front door stood open. My mother waited inside, but she did not come toward me.

She stood beside the old staircase. Her hands were empty. Behind her, the rooms looked warm and ready. I tried to cross the threshold. The floorboards answered with three slow knocks. My mother pointed toward my coat pocket.

I pulled out the key. It had become hot enough to hurt. My mother turned toward the back room. The incense smell thickened around us. Then the lights began going out, one room at a time. She remained beside the last lamp.

At dawn, I woke in my city room. The key lay on the floor beside my bed. My mother's old trunk stood open. Inside was the village house deed and one folded shawl. The promise had found its way back to me.

I drove to the village that same morning. The road had narrowed beneath the trees. The house looked smaller than I remembered. No light showed in the windows. When I unlocked the door, the smell of burnt incense came from the back room.

Nothing moved inside. Dust covered the table. A chair faced the doorway. Beside it sat a bowl with no food in it. I opened every window. The warm air left slowly, carrying the incense scent into the yard.

I spent the night on the floor because the bed felt borrowed. Near midnight, the hallway creaked. I waited for my mother to call me. The sound came again, farther away this time. It stopped beside the locked back room.

The next morning, I found that room open. I had not touched it. My mother's trunk stood inside, exactly as she had left it. The folded clothes were gone. In their place lay a small brass lamp, still warm.
I carried the lamp to the front room. It lit the chair and the wall above it. There was no flame inside. I sat until evening. When darkness came, the lamp went out by itself.
I did not sell the house. I could not leave it locked again. Each week, I repaired one small thing. I fixed the gate. I cleared the roof. I washed the windows that had held those lights in my dreams.
For the first month, I slept there alone. The dreams stopped. So did the incense smell. On the first morning without either, I found the key on the table. It was cold for the first time in ten years.
story.ending: The next morning, I left the city for good. I found work near the village. I kept the house open, though nobody else lived there. Each month, I carried rice to the back room. I lit one stick of incense. The smoke always bent toward the empty chair. My mother had waited ten years. I had waited for a better time. What would you have done?

source.text:
Vell Lane School closed in 1991 after a storm loosened half its roof slates. The district kept the building for storage and assigned a single caretaker to walk the corridors each evening. The registers from its final year were boxed and sent to the county office, where most of them still sit unopened. Two boxes are missing from the sequence.

The final register recorded one teacher and no students for the last three months of term. Attendance lines for that period are ruled but blank. A marginal note, in the teacher's hand, reads that the class had been marked present and dismissed. The note is undated and unsigned. The district office has never been able to explain it.

The building itself has been surveyed twice for damp. Both surveys mention the smell of wet chalk in the east corridor, strongest outside a locked classroom. No chalk was found in the room on either visit. The second survey recommends that the room be opened only in daylight.

The caretaker's logs from 1991 to 1994 are missing. Only the metal cover of the first ledger survives, stamped with the district seal. A plumber who worked in the building in 1996 recalled that the door of the classroom had been painted shut, though the handle still turned.

The county office has no plan for the site. The roof was repaired in 2003 and the gates were chained in 2011. The registers are stored with other school records, and access requires a written request. Few requests are made, and none in the last five years.

story.title: The Attendance List
story.hook: I was the caretaker of an empty school when the blackboard began writing back. Every evening, classroom seven carried the smell of wet chalk, though nobody had entered it for years.
paragraphs: The school had been closed since the roof started leaking. Most windows were boarded from inside. I kept one key ring and a narrow list of jobs. Lock the gates. Check the pipes. Walk the corridors before leaving.

I worked there alone each evening. The building settled around me. Pipes clicked behind the walls. Old radiators gave out small knocks. Those sounds belonged to the place, so I never counted them as company.

The corridor outside classroom seven had one working light. It flickered whenever the wind pressed against the west windows. I replaced the bulb twice. Each time, it worked until I reached the far stairwell.
Classroom seven stayed locked because its ceiling had begun to sag. I checked the handle during every round. Dust lay thick beneath the door. No footprints crossed it, not even mine.

The teacher assigned there had vanished during the final term. I knew that much from an old staff photograph. Her name was written beneath the picture. The ink had faded, but the letters remained clear.
The caretaker before me had left one warning in the maintenance ledger. He wrote that classroom seven should stay closed after sunset. There was no reason beside it. The next page had been torn out.

One wet evening, I found the classroom door open. The corridor light blinked above me. Inside, the blackboard held the teacher’s name in large white letters. The chalk lines shone as though they had just been drawn.
I checked every window first. They were sealed. The only chalk in the room sat inside a locked cupboard. I unlocked it with the master key. The sticks were dry and untouched.
I wiped the name away with a damp cloth. The board squeaked beneath my hand. When I finished, the cloth was warm. The chalk dust on it had turned to a thin paste.
I locked the room and waited in the corridor. Nothing moved inside. Still, the handle pressed down once. It rose slowly, then settled. I heard three soft taps against the blackboard.
The following evening, the name was back. This time, a second line stood beneath it. It read, Please take attendance. I had never seen those words in the old records.

The final register recorded one teacher and no students for the last three months of term. Attendance lines for that period are ruled but blank. A marginal note, in the teacher's hand, reads that the class had been marked present and dismissed. The note is undated and unsigned. The district office has never been able to explain it.
I read the name aloud without meaning to. The corridor light went out. From inside the classroom came the scrape of a chair. Then another. Then many more, moving across the floor.
When the light returned, every desk faced the blackboard. The teacher’s name had been wiped clean. In its place, one line of chalk waited for me. It said, Present.
I left the ledger on the floor and backed away. The door closed before I reached it. Through the wood, I heard a woman turn pages. She stopped at the blank student column.
I did not touch the handle. The light above me flickered in a steady rhythm. Each blink sounded like a small knock. Behind the door, chalk moved across the board.
The writing stopped when the front gate alarm rang. I ran outside and left the building unlocked. From the pavement, I watched the corridor light burn through the boarded windows.
The next morning, I returned with the district manager. Classroom seven was locked again. Dust covered the floor. The ledger lay where I had dropped it, but the final page was no longer blank.
A new entry filled the page. It listed the teacher’s name, then mine. Beside both names, the same word appeared. Present. The ink looked old, though I had never written it.
I handed in my keys that afternoon. The district manager asked why. I told him the pipes were making noises. I did not mention the door, the desks, or the page.
The school has stayed closed since then. I pass it only in daylight. Sometimes classroom seven shows a pale square through the boards. Sometimes the corridor light flickers beneath the door.
story.ending: I stopped wiping the board after that. The name still appears, but only when the corridor light begins to flicker. I leave the room untouched now. By morning, the chalk is always dry. The rest of the school remains silent. Have you ever heard something like this?

source.text:
Phòng lưu trữ của huyện Nghĩa Tân Thượng bắt đầu số hóa hồ sơ đất đai từ đầu năm nay. Toàn bộ tài liệu giấy được chuyển sang một phòng riêng có máy lạnh. Nhóm thực hiện gồm bốn người, trong đó hai người đã làm việc tại phòng hơn mười năm. Kinh phí cho đợt số hóa lấy từ ngân sách huyện.

Mỗi hồ sơ giấy được chụp hai lần để tránh sai sót, sau đó ảnh được kiểm tra lại bởi một người khác. Quy trình này áp dụng cho cả hồ sơ đã được đóng thành tập. Những trang bị rách được đặt trong túi nhựa trước khi chụp. Tài liệu gốc vẫn được giữ tại phòng, không chuyển đi nơi khác.

Thời gian xử lý trung bình là bảy mươi hồ sơ mỗi ngày. Con số này thấp hơn dự kiến vì nhiều hồ sơ phải tháo ghim và làm phẳng giấy. Nhóm thực hiện cho biết sẽ không tăng tiến độ bằng cách bỏ qua bước kiểm tra. Một ngày làm việc chỉ kéo dài đến khi đủ ánh sáng tự nhiên.

Hệ thống lưu ảnh được đặt trên một máy chủ riêng của huyện. Dữ liệu được sao lưu mỗi tuần vào một ổ cứng để trong két của phòng. Bản sao lưu không kết nối với mạng nội bộ. Người dùng chỉ được tra cứu ảnh qua một máy tính đặt tại quầy.

Đợt số hóa đầu tiên dự kiến hoàn thành vào cuối năm sau. Sau đó phòng sẽ chuyển sang hồ sơ hộ tịch, khối lượng lớn hơn nhiều. Người đứng đầu phòng cho biết chưa có kế hoạch cho phép tra cứu từ xa. Mọi yêu cầu tra cứu hiện vẫn phải làm tại quầy.

samples.fact: Mỗi hồ sơ giấy được chụp hai lần để tránh sai sót, sau đó ảnh được kiểm tra lại bởi một người khác.

source.text:
Bến phà Cửa Đôi thay đổi giờ chạy từ ngày mười tháng sáu. Chuyến đầu tiên sẽ khởi hành lúc năm giờ ba mươi phút thay vì năm giờ. Chuyến cuối cùng giữ nguyên giờ cũ là tám giờ tối. Bảng giờ mới được dán tại hai đầu bến và tại quầy bán vé.

Việc thay đổi được đề xuất sau khi bến ghi nhận số khách tăng vào buổi sáng. Trong ba tháng gần nhất, chuyến năm giờ thường chở quá tải. Phà chỉ được phép chở tối đa bốn mươi xe máy và hai xe tải nhỏ. Người điều hành muốn giãn giờ để giảm số người dồn vào một chuyến.

Tuyến phà có hai chiếc, trong đó một chiếc đang được sửa máy từ đầu tháng. Chiếc còn lại phải chạy liên tục trong ngày, kể cả giờ nghỉ trưa. Nếu chiếc đang sửa chưa xong trước ngày đổi giờ, bến sẽ giữ lịch cũ thêm một tuần. Thông báo về việc này sẽ được dán cùng bảng giờ mới.

Giá vé không thay đổi trong đợt điều chỉnh này. Vé tháng vẫn được bán từ ngày hai mươi lăm của tháng trước. Khách đi xe đạp trả nửa giá và không cần đăng ký trước. Trẻ dưới sáu tuổi được miễn vé nhưng phải có người lớn đi cùng.

Bến phà đã nhận được một số ý kiến đề nghị thêm chuyến trưa. Người điều hành cho biết việc này chỉ xem xét sau khi chiếc phà thứ hai hoạt động trở lại. Trong thời gian chờ, khách có thể gửi xe máy theo chuyến hàng của bến. Dịch vụ này đã có từ trước và không cần đặt trước.

samples.fact: Nếu chiếc đang sửa chưa xong trước ngày đổi giờ, bến sẽ giữ lịch cũ thêm một tuần.

source.text:
Xã Đồng Văn Thượng lắp hệ thống loa cảnh báo bão tại bốn điểm trong xã từ năm ngoái. Loa được đặt trên cột bê tông cao sáu mét, gắn pin mặt trời. Mỗi điểm phát được trong phạm vi khoảng bảy trăm mét. Hệ thống do một nhóm kỹ thuật của huyện lắp đặt và bàn giao cho xã quản lý.

Loa được thử vào sáu giờ tối thứ sáu hằng tuần, trong ba mươi giây. Người dân trong xã đã quen với tiếng thử này. Việc thử do một cán bộ của xã thực hiện bằng điện thoại di động. Nếu không nghe thấy tiếng thử, người dân được yêu cầu báo cho trưởng thôn.

Khi có tin bão, loa sẽ phát bản tin ngắn lặp lại mỗi mười lăm phút. Bản tin gồm hướng đi của bão, giờ dự kiến ảnh hưởng và nơi trú tạm. Bản tin được đọc trực tiếp, không dùng giọng tổng hợp. Người đọc là cán bộ phụ trách phòng chống thiên tai của xã.

Hệ thống dùng pin mặt trời nên vẫn hoạt động khi mất điện lưới. Mỗi điểm có một ắc quy dự phòng đủ dùng trong hai ngày. Ắc quy được kiểm tra mỗi tháng và thay sau ba năm. Việc kiểm tra được ghi vào một cuốn sổ đặt tại văn phòng xã.

Trong đợt bão tháng chín, hai trong bốn điểm loa bị mất tiếng do đứt dây. Nhóm kỹ thuật của huyện đã sửa trong vòng hai ngày. Xã đang đề nghị thay dây trên toàn bộ bốn điểm bằng loại dây bọc dày hơn. Kinh phí dự kiến được lấy từ quỹ phòng chống thiên tai của huyện.

samples.fact: Khi có tin bão, loa sẽ phát bản tin ngắn lặp lại mỗi mười lăm phút. Bản tin gồm hướng đi của bão, giờ dự kiến ảnh hưởng và nơi trú ẩn.

source.text:
